newsitem.title: USA: GFOA calls '97 make-or-break year on flow control.
newsitem.headline: GFOA calls '97 make-or-break year on flow control.

text.p: If the U.S. Congress does not enact "flow control" relief for states and localities this year, it probably never will, a Government Finance Officers Association official said Tuesday.
"If it doesn't happen this year, it may never happen," Catherine Spain, head of GFOA's Washington liaison office, told finance officers meeting here for the group's 91st annual conference.

Flow control refers to the ability of local governments to require that muni solid waste generated within a jurisdication be processed at designated disposal sites. Since 1980, over $24 billion in muni bonds have been issued to pay for construction of solid waste facilities.

The U.S. Supreme Court in its 1994 decision in C&A Carbone, Inc. v. Clarkstown, N.Y. struck down flow control as unconstitutional, triggering a number of solid waste debt downgrades by bond rating agencies.

Since 1994, several bills have been introduced to extend flow control authority, but none has passed. Sen. John Chafee, R-R.I., who chairs a key Senate panel with jurisdiction over the issue, has circulated a draft bill to extend only limited flow control authority. Chafee is expected to formally introduce the bill shortly.
"I think we are at the point now where the bill is so watered down that it's going to be very narrow," Spain said. "(And) if it doesn't happen this year, I don't think" it ever will, she said.
